statement: The system shall accept trading instructions from the client-facing service.
The system shall validate trading instructions to ensure they are complete and authorized.
The system shall classify trading instructions into the correct order type.
The system shall support the order types buy, sell, amend, and cancel.
The system shall apply trading rules to determine whether compatible orders can be matched.
The system shall carry out the match and record the result when compatible orders can be matched.
The system shall leave an order open or reject it when compatible orders cannot be matched, depending on the instruction and rule outcome.
The system shall publish the trading outcome to the rest of the platform.
The system shall keep its own records so authorized managers can inspect what happened later.
The interview scope shall focus on the Central Trading System itself.
The Central Trading System shall receive trading instructions.
The Central Trading System shall process orders.
The Central Trading System shall match orders.
The Central Trading System shall share results with other parts of the platform.
Managers shall be able to inspect the Central Trading System.
The interviewee is speaking as the business stakeholder for the trading platform.
The subsystem needs to support trading operations and oversight.
Instructions shall come in from the client-facing service and be handed to the trading engine for processing.
The system shall determine what kind of instruction it is.
The system shall apply the relevant trading rules.
The system shall match compatible buy and sell orders when possible.
The system shall centralize matching and processing.

Additional requirements beyond the main ones, such as performance targets, detailed audit behavior, or special exception handling, must be confirmed with the trading and compliance teams before being treated as requirements.
The system shall include an audit trail.
Authorized people shall be able to trace an order from receipt through processing to the final outcome.
The audit trail shall not expose the decision path to everyone.
The system shall control access using role-based access control.
Only approved system managers or designated support staff shall be able to view the audit trail and other manager-facing information.
The exact roles and approval process shall match the internal security policy.
The system shall prioritize centralized instruction processing and matching as the first main feature.
The system shall provide clear handling when an instruction cannot be matched or cannot be processed as expected.
If an instruction cannot be matched, it should be kept as pending or queued until a compatible order arrives, provided that the trading rules allow it.
If an instruction cannot be processed because it is invalid or incomplete, it should be rejected with a clear reason sent back through the platform.
Matching compatible orders is the highest priority.
Rejecting invalid or incomplete instructions is important.
Queuing pending orders is lower priority than actual matching and validation behavior.
The system shall send the trade result and any relevant status back to the client-facing service and any internal services that need it.
The system shall make confirmations available promptly so the rest of the platform can act on them.
The system shall make rejections available promptly so the rest of the platform can act on them.
The system shall make pending status updates available promptly so the rest of the platform can act on them.
The system shall keep information consistent across systems to avoid conflicting views of the same order.
The client-facing service team should be considered because they see how instructions enter the system and how responses need to come back.
Compliance or risk stakeholders should be considered.
Trading systems usually need strong traceability.
Trading systems usually need controls around order handling.
Operations or support staff should be considered.
Operations or support staff are likely to investigate exceptions.
Operations or support staff are likely to investigate failed instructions.
Operations or support staff are likely to investigate audit trail entries.
The Central Trading System shall operate the core flows in production with no major defects.
The system shall handle processing and result distribution quickly enough for trading operations.
The system shall provide clear exception handling if any downstream service is unavailable.
The system shall indicate whether results were delivered or need to be retried when a downstream service is unavailable.
The system shall take incoming instructions from the client-facing service.
The system shall determine what kind of order or instruction has been received.
The system shall apply trading rules to determine whether an order or instruction can be matched.
The system shall pass match information or trade state changes onward so the rest of the platform stays in sync.
The system shall support faster trading.
The system shall provide managers with visibility into the system.
The central trading system shall validate incoming instructions.
The central trading system shall only process requests it is authorized to handle.
The central trading system shall record enough information for audit and operational review.
The central trading system shall support inspection by system managers without exposing information they should not see.
The central trading system shall handle exceptions or failed matches cleanly.
Client-facing inputs to the central trading system shall be treated as instructions to validate and classify first.
The central trading system shall refuse incomplete client-facing requests rather than pushing them further into matching.
Once an order is accepted, the central trading system shall hand off the resulting trade or order-state changes to downstream services such as clearing or settlement.
The central trading system shall not perform clearing or settlement functions itself.
The central trading system shall handle requests that are already in a terminal state differently from fresh orders.
The central trading system shall handle duplicate or conflicting instructions differently from fresh orders.
The central trading system shall handle matching and state decisions, then publish the outcome onward.
Orders and trading instructions shall be received through the client-facing service.
End users shall not interact with the central trading system directly.
Authorized trading clients or broker-side users shall be able to originate instructions.
The platform shall allow only authenticated and permitted actors to submit instructions into the flow.
The trading subsystem shall be available whenever the trading window is open.
During service interruptions, the trading subsystem shall stop accepting new instructions.
The trading subsystem may have cutoffs around market close, maintenance periods, or instrument-specific trading windows.
If the service is down or recovering, the trading subsystem shall clearly indicate that it cannot process new trading activity until it is back in a safe state.
The trading subsystem shall fit into the broader trading platform.
The trading subsystem shall operate reliably at low latency.
The trading subsystem shall be deployable in a controlled environment that meets security and resilience expectations.
The system shall keep an auditable record of accepted orders.
The business shall be able to trace what happened and why from the auditable record.
The system shall apply retention controls in accordance with applicable internal compliance requirements and market regulations.
The system shall apply access controls in accordance with applicable internal compliance requirements and market regulations.
The system shall remain stable for the core flow of order intake, validation, matching, and trade publication when new products or order types are added.
The system should support additional markets in the future.
The system should support more complex order conditions in the future.
The system should support higher throughput in the future.
The system shall preserve correct matching behavior as the rules evolve.
Trading rules shall not be expected to change on a daily basis.
Trading rules shall change when there is a market rule update, a new product launch, or a major business change.
Trading rule changes shall be more occasional than regular operational tweaking.
Some trading rule parameters may need adjustment more often than the underlying matching logic.
The system shall only match orders that are compatible on the instrument.
The system shall only match orders that are compatible on price.
The system shall only match orders that are compatible on quantity.
The system shall only match orders that are compatible on side.
A buy order can only match a sell order under the applicable trading rules.
The system shall respect the configured order priority rules.
The default order priority rules are price first and then time.
The system shall allow a specific market rule to override the default order priority rules.
The system shall not match any order that violates the current trading constraints.
The system shall reject an instruction immediately if it is missing the required instrument detail.
The system shall reject an instruction immediately if it is missing the required side detail.
The system shall reject an instruction immediately if it is missing the required quantity detail.
The system shall reject an instruction immediately if it is missing a usable price when a price is needed.
The system shall refuse obviously invalid requests immediately.
The system shall refuse requests with malformed values immediately.
The system shall refuse duplicate requests that would create conflicting orders.
The system shall refuse instructions that violate current trading status or permissions.
The system shall stop a request before matching if it is outside allowed trading hours.
The system shall stop a request before matching if the account is not authorized for the activity.
If an order is rejected or remains unfilled with no trade to report, there may be nothing to send to clearing or settlement.
Matching shall be the system’s main responsibility.
Trading must continue functioning without interruptions during the initial deployment and cutover.
The system must provide trustworthy executions from day one.
The initial deployment and cutover must use a controlled cutover.
The initial deployment and cutover must include enough testing.
The initial deployment and cutover must include a clear rollback plan.
The system must be closely monitored immediately after go-live so that matching or messaging issues are caught quickly.
Users and downstream teams must know exactly what changed.
Small differences in order handling can create confusion.
The Central Trading System shall bring over some legacy data at cutover.
The Central Trading System shall make any open orders available on day one.
The Central Trading System shall make active positions or exposures relevant to current trading available on day one.
The Central Trading System shall make whatever audit history is needed for reconciliation and inspection available on day one.
The Central Trading System may leave closed or very old records in the source system or archive them separately, depending on retention rules.
The Central Trading System shall clearly mark imported records as migrated so that they are not treated as fresh trading activity.
The business shall agree on which records are authoritative after cutover.
Cutoff dates and retention rules shall be agreed with compliance and operations.
An order shall be defined as the trading intent after the system has accepted and normalized the request.
A match shall be defined as the result of pairing two compatible orders under the trading rules.
A match shall produce an actual execution.
The workflow shall receive a request in, validate and handle the order in the central system, and produce a match or execution out if there is a compatible counter-order.
A new order shall start fresh trading interest.
A cancel shall withdraw an existing live order.
An amend shall change an existing order’s terms only if that is still allowed by the trading rules.
If the service is impaired, the system shall either queue incoming orders or reject them depending on issue severity and whether ordering can be preserved safely.
If the system cannot guarantee correct processing or a reliable recovery position, it shall reject incoming orders rather than accept them.

The system shall resume normal processing only when the trading window is still open, the system state is verified clean, and downstream interfaces are healthy enough to process outcomes without losing or duplicating activity.
A cancel or amend instruction shall only be accepted if the target order is still live and eligible under the trading rules.
Intake rules may differ depending on whether an instruction arrives during a pause, a recovery period, or a normal open trading state.
Intake rules depend on both the current order state and the current market state.
The system shall reject orders that violate basic business limits on quantity at intake.
The system shall reject orders that violate basic business limits on price at intake.
The system shall reject orders that violate instrument-specific constraints at intake.
The system shall prevent the same order from entering twice when duplicate submissions occur due to client service retries after a timeout.
The system shall perform reference data checks to confirm that the instrument exists and that the participant is allowed to trade it.
The system shall apply some rules in a non-global way rather than making all intake limits and duplicate checks fully global.
The system shall apply basic format validation and duplicate detection system-wide.
The system shall apply quantity-related rules based on the instrument.
The system shall apply price band rules based on the instrument.
The system shall apply some eligibility thresholds based on the instrument, the participant, and sometimes the order type.
The system shall apply a common baseline first and then look up the relevant rules for the specific order context.
The system shall refuse a request if the order type is restricted for the account or venue.
The matching process shall operate as close to real time as practical during peak periods.
If processing slows enough to risk stale prices, the system shall not continue processing at the same pace.

In conditions where processing slows enough to risk stale prices, missed priorities, or inconsistent sequencing, the system shall hold, queue, or temporarily reject new intake depending on the condition.
The latency target has not yet been specified precisely.
Business correctness shall take priority over processing everything slowly.
When the slowdown is minor and recovery is expected quickly, the system should queue a limited amount of new intake to preserve order of arrival.
The exact intake-handling behavior should depend on the severity of the slowdown and whether the system can still guarantee fairness and correct sequencing.
A new market or order condition shall only be enabled after its rules are fully configured, tested, and traceable in the system’s reference data.
The matching engine shall treat a new market or order condition as a distinct rule set so that sequencing and audit logs remain consistent.
Downstream notifications shall carry enough context for other services to interpret the result correctly.
Manager review shall be able to see what was applied, what was rejected, and why.
When a new market is turned on, the system shall ensure that nothing becomes opaque to manager review.
The system shall require business approval before activating a new market or order condition.
The system shall require testing in a non-production environment before activating a new market or order condition.
The system shall require verification that reference data and trading rules are complete and consistent before activating a new market or order condition.
The system shall require sign-off that downstream systems can interpret any new status or notification fields associated with a new market or order condition before activation.
The system shall keep a new market or order condition inactive if any critical pieces are missing.
The system shall not activate a new market or order condition unless correct matching and end-to-end auditability can be guaranteed.
A new market or condition shall get its own distinct rule set if it changes how orders are prioritized.
A cosmetic or reporting variation may use an existing rule set if the underlying trading behavior is truly the same.
The system shall use the gating condition of whether applying the old rules would change business outcomes or create ambiguity in audit and review.
Any mismatch between what was approved and what is actually configured shall block activation.
Nothing shall go live unless the whole chain is consistent and auditable.
When the service cannot safely process trading, the system shall not accept new instructions for matching.
If it is still safe and within the allowed window, the system may queue new instructions.
If processing cannot resume promptly, the system shall reject new instructions.
The system shall enforce cutoffs around market close and scheduled maintenance windows.
The system shall support instrument-specific trading hours.
Outside the allowed trading windows, the system shall hold or reject an instruction according to the trading rule for the relevant market.
An instruction shall be eligible for intake only when the market is open for that instrument and the order is in a normal new or re-submitted state.
Holding a potentially valid instruction when the market is temporarily unavailable shall be allowed only if that is part of the approved operating rule for that market.
All three record types shall include a unique identifier.
All three record types shall include timestamps.
All three record types shall include market or instrument details.
All three record types shall include participant or account context.
All three record types shall include the current status.
All three record types shall include a link back to the originating instruction.
All three record types shall include sufficient pricing and quantity information to reconstruct what happened.
All three record types shall include an audit trail of who or what caused each change.
An order record shall focus on the original intent and lifecycle.
A match record shall capture the pairing logic and the two sides that were matched.
An execution record shall capture the final fills and any quantity or price actually executed.
Downstream systems shall receive the key identifiers and outcome fields in a consistent format.
If matching or outbound messaging behaves unexpectedly after go-live, rollback shall be immediate when there is any risk of incorrect trades.
If matching or outbound messaging behaves unexpectedly after go-live, rollback shall be immediate when there is any risk of duplicate messages or loss of audit trail.
If an issue is limited and can be safely contained without affecting trade integrity, the cutover may be held and the issue fixed forward.
The decision to hold the cutover and fix forward shall depend on issue severity and whether operations can guarantee that no bad output has escaped.
If an instruction arrives just before the market window ends and there is still enough time to process it safely under that market's rules, the system shall accept it and handle it normally.

If there is not enough time to complete matching before cutoff, or the market closes while the instruction is pending, the system shall hold the instruction only when the approved rule allows late processing.

If there is not enough time to complete matching before cutoff, or the market closes while the instruction is pending, the system shall reject the instruction when the approved rule does not allow late processing.

During a short maintenance interruption, the system should prefer holding an instruction rather than rejecting it, as long as the instruction is still valid and processing can resume within the allowed operational window.
The system's behavior for these cases shall be consistent per market or instrument.
If a new market or higher volume would strain current processing, the system should throttle, queue, or partition safely.
If a new market or higher volume would strain current processing, the system should not allow incomplete matches or dropped notifications.
When scaling is paused or capped, it shall remain so until behavior is confirmed to be correct.

When instability, unexplained latency, backlog growth, or possible divergence in matching or outbound notifications is present, the system shall use a slower but safer path instead of pushing through.
The system shall slow down when a new market is in a heightened verification period.
The system shall keep matching results exactly consistent with the approved trading rules.
Normal throughput shall only be restored after the underlying issue is cleared.
Normal throughput restoration shall require confirmation that matching, record creation, and outbound notifications are all still producing the expected results.
If the pause was triggered by a rule change or a new market being introduced, the slower path shall only be lifted once the change has been validated in production conditions.
The system shall record the failure clearly.
The system shall mark the affected order or match state.
The system shall send a structured exception message to downstream systems that need to know.
The system shall not stop unrelated orders or matching activity from continuing.
If an exception affects trading integrity, the system shall halt or isolate only the affected flow rather than the whole platform.
If an exception affects trading integrity, the system shall escalate to operations immediately.
If an exception is non-blocking, the system shall make it visible in the audit trail and monitoring so it can be reviewed later.
The system shall allow filtering by order status.
The system shall allow filtering by market.
The system shall allow filtering by time range.
The system shall allow filtering by instrument.
The system shall allow filtering by exception type for investigating failures.
The system shall allow filtering by account or client reference for investigating a specific trading relationship.

The system shall determine exception handling based on whether the exception is local to one order or one instrument, or whether it affects the integrity of matching or outbound reporting more broadly.
If an exception is isolated and recoverable, the system shall notify only the systems that need to act on the specific order, and the rest of trading shall continue.
If an exception could cause incorrect matches, missing records, or broken downstream messages, the system shall escalate it immediately to operations and isolate the affected flow.
The system shall base the exception-handling decision on severity and business impact rather than on a fixed one-size-fits-all rule.
The system shall escalate an inbound instruction exception when the exception rate crosses a threshold.
The system shall escalate an inbound instruction exception when the same instruction keeps failing repeatedly.
The system shall escalate an inbound instruction exception when there is any sign that the issue is systemic rather than isolated.
The system shall immediately escalate an inbound instruction exception if the exception points to bad data.
The system shall immediately escalate an inbound instruction exception if the exception indicates a rule violation.
The system shall immediately escalate an inbound instruction exception if it could affect matching correctness or downstream notification integrity.
The system shall use local notification only for a one-off, clearly contained issue that can be retried or corrected without impacting the wider flow.
The system shall escalate an inbound instruction exception when it cannot confidently classify the issue.
Some views of the subsystem’s trading information shall be broader than others.
The system may require approval-based restrictions for especially sensitive information.
The permitted originator of a trading instruction shall depend on the instruction type and the permissions attached to the client or broker user.
Basic order instructions should usually be allowed for ordinary trading clients.
Instructions that change an existing order should be limited to users with the appropriate authority.
Instructions that cancel an existing order should be limited to users with the appropriate authority.
Instructions that override an existing order should be limited to users with the appropriate authority.
Some instruction categories should require additional approval or a higher privilege level before they can enter the flow.
The system shall support delegated approvers as an actor category permitted to originate instructions under specific conditions.
The system shall allow a delegated approver to originate an instruction only when a workflow requires a second level of authorization.
The system shall support system-operated accounts as an actor category with limited permissions.
The system shall limit a system account to controlled operational tasks such as automated corrections or routed exceptions.
The system shall not allow a system account to perform normal discretionary trading.
The system shall allow supervisors to originate or release instructions only when their role explicitly permits it.
The system shall apply an audit-heavy approval rule when supervisors originate or release instructions.
The business rule for originating instructions shall be based on role, context, and authority level.
Access to the most sensitive views shall require a higher clearance level and a business justification.
Access to the most sensitive views shall sometimes require temporary approval from a senior operations or compliance lead.
Detailed exception traces shall be treated as sensitive content for access control purposes.
Counterparty-identifying data shall be treated as sensitive content for access control purposes.
Information tied to investigations shall be treated as sensitive content for access control purposes.
Some categories of information shall remain inaccessible to otherwise authorized managers unless they have a specific elevated role.
Sealed audit material shall remain inaccessible to otherwise authorized managers unless they have a specific elevated role.
Confidential client data beyond what managers need for operations shall remain inaccessible to otherwise authorized managers unless they have a specific elevated role.
Security-related details that could expose internal controls shall remain inaccessible to otherwise authorized managers unless they have a specific elevated role.
Only people with a named elevated role and a documented need to know shall be allowed to access the manager-excluded categories.
Access to the manager-excluded categories shall normally be granted only through an approval path tied to a specific case, incident, or investigation.
Standing manager access shall not be used to grant access to the manager-excluded categories.
Emergency overrides shall be limited to a narrow set of senior roles.
Emergency overrides shall be time-limited, logged, and reviewed afterward.
Emergency overrides shall be exceptional and not part of routine operations.
A named elevated role must not bypass controls when the data category is explicitly restricted by policy or regulation.
The person requesting emergency access should ideally not be the same person who approves it.
Emergency access may be approved only when there is an active incident or business-critical outage and the access is necessary to restore service or assess impact.
At the time of access, the system shall capture the reason for the emergency access.
At the time of access, the system shall capture the start and end time of the emergency access.
At the time of access, the system shall capture what was viewed or changed during the emergency access.
The system shall capture access details whenever access is granted outside normal standing permission.
The system shall capture access details for pre-approved maintenance windows.
The system shall allow a lighter access record for pre-approved maintenance windows than for a true emergency case.
The system shall not capture unnecessary personal detail about the requester beyond what is needed for audit.
The access record for routine low-impact incidents may be simpler.
If a prerequisite is only partially ready, cutover should proceed only when the missing part is non-blocking and there is a documented workaround that keeps trading safe and traceable.
If a partially ready prerequisite affects order integrity, matching accuracy, or the ability to stop trading cleanly, cutover should not proceed.
The go/no-go call should be made by the designated cutover lead.
The designated cutover lead should make the go/no-go call only after sign-off from operations and the business owner or trading control representative.
During the first live trades, the designated cutover lead should coordinate monitoring.
During the first live trades, the designated cutover lead should be able to halt the rollout immediately if something looks wrong.

The cutover lead may make the go/no-go call without waiting for the usual sign-offs only when there is a time-critical issue and waiting for the usual sign-offs would create a bigger operational or market risk than proceeding or stopping immediately.

This exception is expected to be limited to situations such as a live trading window, a settlement cutoff, or a system instability where an immediate decision is needed to protect order integrity or customer impact.
The cutover lead's emergency decision must be bounded by pre-agreed emergency criteria.
Anything that creates an immediate risk of financial loss should count as an emergency.
A regulatory breach should count as an emergency.
An unrecoverable data inconsistency should count as an emergency.
A serious security issue should count as an emergency.
Evidence that orders are being routed or matched incorrectly should count as an emergency.
A failure in monitoring that prevents safe observation of live trades should count as an emergency.
The emergency path should remain narrow and be reserved for situations where waiting would clearly be worse.
If a new market or condition changes the core matching logic, priority order, eligibility rules, or timing in a way that could affect execution outcomes, it should have its own rule set.

If a new market or condition only changes a parameter such as a threshold, trading session window, or a small exception that does not alter the matching flow, it can usually be handled by extending an existing rule set.
The main test for deciding whether a new market or condition needs its own rule set is whether the change could produce different match results or audit treatment.
If a change could produce different match results or audit treatment, it should be isolated so it is clear, reviewable, and easier to govern.
The system shall record who approved the emergency access incident.
The system shall record who actually used the emergency access.
The system shall record the incident or ticket number for the emergency access incident.
If changes were made during emergency access, the system shall record what was changed at a high level.
If changes were made during emergency access, the system shall record a reference to the audit log entry.
The first delivery shall include explicit cancellation handling for incoming instructions and matched orders.
The first delivery shall include explicit rejection handling for incoming instructions and matched orders.
The first delivery shall specify how the system handles orders that must be rejected for rule or validation reasons.
The system shall define an end state for a trade instruction that does not proceed normally.
The first release shall focus on the straight-through trading path and the essential reject or cancel outcomes.
Detailed handling of non-standard outcomes, including richer user messaging, specialized exception workflows, and a broader set of edge-case statuses, shall be deferred to a later phase.
The core audit trail and downstream notifications shall continue to work in the first release.
Later phases shall refine the non-standard outcomes without changing the fundamental matching engine.
The Central Trading System shall be the core matching component inside the broader trading platform.
The Central Trading System shall take orders coming in from the client-facing service.
The Central Trading System shall identify what kind of trading instruction each incoming order is.
The Central Trading System shall match compatible stock orders according to the trading rules in force.
Front-end services shall not make matching decisions themselves.
The Central Trading System shall provide a central place where resulting trade information can be passed to the rest of the platform.
The Central Trading System shall allow resulting trade information to be reviewed by authorized managers.
The system shall support higher trading volume with more consistency and less manual intervention.
The system shall provide faster order handling.
The system shall provide cleaner auditability.
The system shall provide a more reliable path for passing trade outcomes to downstream systems.
The system shall remain responsive and compliant as activity grows and the market becomes more demanding.
The system shall enforce the same trading rules everywhere through one central matching service.
The system shall prioritize order processing speed as a key performance indicator.
The system shall prioritize matching accuracy as a key performance indicator.
The system shall prioritize system availability during trading hours as a key performance indicator.
The system shall measure how quickly confirmed trades are propagated to the rest of the platform.
Operations staff shall be able to inspect what happened without needing manual support.
Exact target numbers for these metrics are not yet defined and must be confirmed with the business team.
The Central Trading System shall support authorized system managers who review system information and trade activity.
The Central Trading System shall provide fast order handling for the client service.
The Central Trading System shall support traceability for system managers.
Operations and compliance interact with the Central Trading System.
Operations staff may need visibility into queues, failures, and unusual matching behavior.
Compliance or audit reviewers may need read-only access to records and reports.
The needs of operations and compliance are more about transparency than placing trades.
Downstream services shall prioritize receiving accurate trade data.
Auditors may rely on exported records or reports as an external stakeholder group.
Operations staff shall mostly monitor the system.
Compliance officers shall usually not use the system for live trading.
System managers shall have the broadest access for inspection and support.
External auditors shall be able to review trade histories, rule application evidence, timestamps, and exception logs.
External auditor review of system records shall be periodic and tied to audit cycles or a specific investigation.
The system shall handle cancellations and amendments received before execution during a normal trading day.
The system shall react to market open and close times.
The system shall vary matching behavior and permitted actions depending on the trading session.
The system shall be affected by special market conditions such as halts or pauses.
During pre-open or close sessions, the system may restrict what can be accepted or when matching is allowed.
During pre-open or close sessions, the system may queue some instructions until the session changes.
If the market is halted or paused, the system may hold or reject new instructions depending on the rule.
The system should treat market orders as more time-sensitive during live trading.
The system should hold some limit or cancellation instructions until the session allows them.
During halts, the system should queue or block new actions until trading resumes.
The system shall compare order price when determining whether orders can be matched.
The system shall compare order quantity when determining whether orders can be matched.
The system shall apply the configured market priority rules when determining whether orders can be matched.
The system shall execute an order only when the current trading session permits execution.
The system shall treat trading session state as a hard control on order processing.
The system shall stop or constrain matching during special market events such as halts, suspensions, or exceptional volatility conditions according to the market's trading rules.
The exact matching conditions for special market events shall be defined by the exchange or business owners.
The Central Trading System shall keep a complete audit trail of incoming instructions.
The Central Trading System shall keep a complete audit trail of matching decisions.
The Central Trading System shall keep a complete audit trail of executions.
The Central Trading System shall keep a complete audit trail of rejections.
The Central Trading System shall keep a complete audit trail of any manual interventions.
The Central Trading System shall support data retention requirements.
The Central Trading System shall support access control requirements.
The system shall manage trading instructions.
The system shall manage orders.
The system shall manage executed trades.
The system shall manage related status or event records for trading instructions, orders, and executed trades.
A trading instruction shall include instrument details.
A trading instruction shall include side information.
A trading instruction shall include quantity.
A trading instruction shall include price.
A trading instruction shall include the time received.
A trading instruction shall include the submitter identity.
A trade record shall capture the matched result.
A trade record shall capture execution timestamps.
The system shall expect reference data for trading sessions.
The system shall expect reference data for market status.
The data formats shall be aligned with whatever the upstream client service and downstream market systems expect.
The system shall validate received orders.
The system shall enter an order into the matching flow only if it can be matched.
The system shall update an order status as it progresses through partial or full execution.
The system shall move an order into an archive or retention store when it is no longer active.
The system shall not delete an order immediately when it is no longer active.
The system shall determine purge timing according to compliance rules and operational policy.
The downstream components that receive trade results or status changes may include settlement functions, risk functions, and reporting functions.
The interface style between the Central Trading System and its external systems may be messaging, service calls, or both.
The system shall meet strict latency and message integrity expectations for trading communication.
The system shall support near-real-time communication for order acceptance and execution updates.
The interface design shall include acknowledgement behavior.
The interface design shall include error handling behavior.
The interface design shall include recovery behavior.
The system shall interface with a client-facing service that submits instructions and receives acknowledgements, rejections, and execution updates.
The system interfaces shall support low latency.
The system interfaces shall support dependable delivery.
The system interfaces shall support clear message correlation.
The system shall favor fast synchronous acknowledgements for inbound instructions.
The system shall provide durable event delivery for outbound updates.
The system shall use retries.
The system shall use correlation IDs.
The system shall support idempotent handling to protect against duplicates.
The system shall be continuously available when trading is open.
Any planned downtime shall be scheduled outside trading hours and be tightly controlled.
Failover shall occur quickly and with minimal disruption.
The Central Trading System should scale for both normal flow and burst activity.
Surrounding services and event handling should use horizontal scaling.
Core matching behavior should be scaled in a controlled manner rather than being freely load balanced like a stateless web service.
Capacity should expand ahead of peak periods and recover afterward without manual rework.
Security for the subsystem shall be strict because it handles trading instructions and audit trails.
Only authenticated services and approved system managers shall be able to access the subsystem.
Access to the subsystem shall be limited by role so users can only see or do what they are permitted to.
The system shall use encryption in transit.
The system shall provide strong audit logging.
The system shall monitor for unusual access or message activity.
Service-to-service authentication shall be mandatory for the external client-facing service and internal platform services.
Service-to-service authentication should use certificates or another strong machine identity mechanism.
The system shall monitor abnormal message volumes.
